title: One drug, a higher price per claim, or a large share of the State
question: Where was a San Francisco biller paid far more per claim line for a drug product than billers elsewhere in the country, or did it take a large share of all California Medicaid money for that product?
finding: 12 San Francisco billing numbers show a product-year with $100,000 or more at three or more times the rest of the country’s payment per claim line for the same product, or with a quarter or more of California’s money for a product that 20 or more California billers are paid for (7 outside City government and the University); the largest is SF ROYAL MEDICAL SUPPLY, INC, $508,891 in 2019 for drug product code 85645-0002 (no name for this code in the files on disk) (29% of all California Medicaid money for this product that year, among 22 California billers).
how: The national file (21,515,000 rows, one per billing number, prescribing number, drug code and month, 2018 to 2024) was read straight from the zip. 1,135,323 rows whose drug code is one digit repeated, a placeholder for a missing code, were dropped as the federal documentation advises: they carry a sum of $20,382.56 billion, which is not real money. A provider number counts as San Francisco when the California part of the national provider registry puts its practice address in San Francisco (252 billing numbers with drug money); California peers are all billing numbers in that registry file. A drug product is the first nine digits of the code (maker and product), package sizes added together; names come from Open Payments and Part D files that print a name beside a code. The national figure for a product is all money divided by all claim lines for it that year with the biller itself taken out, and needs 500 or more lines. Each biller is shown on its largest flagged product-year.
limits: Nothing here names or counts a patient; the file withholds small cells. The file mixes pharmacy claims with drugs given in clinics and amounts health plans report, does not drop denied claims, and counts claim lines, not quantities: a line for a 90-day supply or a high dose costs more without anything being wrong. Beneficiary-months add up each month’s count of people, so a person treated every month counts twelve times. A specialty pharmacy serving people with HIV, hepatitis or cancer, a hospital clinic, a fertility or eye practice will rightly stand far above an ordinary pharmacy. 2024 is preliminary. The registry places a provider by its address today. Package sizes of one product were added together, so a biller dispensing larger packs shows a higher figure per line. A large share of California can simply mean the biller is the main clinic for that treatment.
